headline: X added GrokAnalyzeWeight parameter at zero, preparing new ranking signal
stat: GrokAnalyzeWeight arrived at 0.0 on November 3, 2026
statContext: New term in X's value model scoring, thirteenth weight parameter
why: X's open-source repo shows a new grok_analyze score entering the weighted sum of predictions that rank posts. The weight is at zero, meaning it adds nothing to scores yet, but the infrastructure is live. This is a dry run: X is testing the plumbing for a new signal without flipping it on. The repo does not define what user action it predicts or whether it measures content understanding, toxicity, or something else, but X rarely adds infrastructure it doesn't plan to use. When the weight goes positive, a new factor will shape For You distribution, likely connected to Grok's content-analysis…
move: Monitor the xai-org/x-algorithm repo for the next weight change. When GrokAnalyzeWeight rises above zero, audit your recent posts using X's Under the Hood tool to see if the new signal tags your content, then test how different post types score under the new factor.

headline: EU demands TikTok deprioritize viewing time, strengthen Not Interested controls
stat: EU says viewing time outweighs explicit user preferences
statContext: European Commission preliminary finding on For You feed, November 6, 2026
why: The European Commission preliminarily found that TikTok's algorithm prioritizes watch time over user requests to see less of certain content. When users tap Not Interested, similar videos keep appearing because the algorithm weights viewing behavior more heavily than stated preferences. Brussels says this creates harmful rabbit holes, especially around mental health and body image content, and demands TikTok give more weight to explicit user controls, remove viewing time as a recommendation signal, and regularly test for harmful patterns. TikTok disputes the finding and has not announced any…
move: No immediate action until TikTok responds and the Commission issues a final decision. If the ruling stands, expect TikTok to roll out new preference controls in the EU, and watch for whether similar pressure spreads to US or UK regulators. Continue optimizing for watch time globally, but prepare for a potential shift toward explicit engagement signals like shares and saves if regulatory pressure…

headline: LinkedIn native video gets 3x reach over text, but views dropped 36% year-over-year
stat: Video views down 36% YoY, engagement up only 7%
statContext: SocialInsider analysis of 1.3 million LinkedIn business page posts, 2024 to 2026
why: LinkedIn's algorithm heavily favors native video in 2026, with multiple sources reporting 3x the organic reach of text posts and a strong dwell-time boost. But SocialInsider's dataset shows video views per post dropped 36% year-over-year across all page sizes, while per-video engagement rose only 7%. The gap is explained by supply: brands are producing more video, so each video fights a bigger pool for the same audience. The reach advantage is real, but the window is closing as competition increases. LinkedIn is actively routing attention away from company pages toward personal profiles, and…
move: Post native video on LinkedIn if you have the production capacity, but prioritize personal profiles over company pages. A mid-level employee with 2,000 connections now typically outreaches a company page with 200,000 followers. If budget is constrained, invest in document-style carousel posts, which outperform video on engagement rate per impression at lower production cost.

sources.title: LinkedIn algorithm and video reach analysis

headline: X switched default ad blending from multi_risk to slot_spread on October 31
stat: ads blender changed from multi_risk to slot_spread
statContext: default configuration parameter in X's published algorithm code on October 31, 2026
why: The published code diff shows X changed how it interleaves ads into the For You feed. The multi_risk blender previously distributed ads based on engagement risk scoring; slot_spread appears to distribute ads at fixed positions regardless of content risk. This likely means ads now appear at predetermined scroll positions rather than being inserted where they fit the engagement pattern. The change suggests X is prioritizing ad visibility and revenue predictability over user experience optimization. However, the RAMGPT audit explicitly notes this is a default parameter change in the mirrored…
move: Test whether your organic posts see different reach patterns around typical ad positions. If slot_spread is live, high-engagement posts might now sit adjacent to ads more often, potentially benefiting from spillover attention or suffering from ad fatigue.

headline: X turned on high-risk video carousel filtering by default on October 31
stat: EnableVideoCarouselHighRiskFilter flag changed from false to true
statContext: default setting in X's published algorithm source code as of October 31, 2026
why: X's algorithm now filters out high-risk videos from appearing in the video carousel feed by default. The flag name suggests X is applying a safety or quality filter to prevent problematic video content from surfacing in a dedicated video browsing experience. This is separate from the main For You feed. The mechanism likely works by flagging videos that trigger spam, harassment, or misinformation classifiers, then excluding them from the carousel. Since this is a new default, it means X is tightening video distribution for content it considers risky, even if that content isn't removed…
move: If you post video on X and notice carousel reach dropping while For You reach holds steady, audit your content against X's safety policies. Avoid borderline topics, unverified claims, or engagement bait that might trigger risk classifiers.

headline: X launched invite-only Video Kickstart Bonus paying creators for 15 vertical videos monthly
stat: 15 qualifying videos on 15 different days earns a monthly bonus
statContext: new invite-only pilot program announced by X in late October 2026
why: X is directly paying select creators to post original vertical video under three minutes, posted one per day for 15 days each program period of roughly one month. This is X's attempt to compete with TikTok and Instagram Reels for short-form video talent by offering guaranteed cash rather than ad revenue share. The invite-only structure means X is hand-picking creators it wants on the platform. The vertical-only requirement and three-minute cap signal X wants to establish a native short-form video culture, not just host YouTube or TikTok exports. Creators can repost their own videos from other…
move: If you get invited, post your best-performing Reels and TikToks to X as well. The requirement is 15 videos on 15 different days, not 15 unique videos, so you can republish. Track whether X distribution improves for paid program participants versus organic-only accounts.

headline: YouTube Shorts videos losing viewers at 10-20% runtime got 39% fewer views on promise channels
stat: 39% fewer views per day
statContext: 2,597 Shorts from 11 channels measured October 2026, controlling for length and average retention
why: On channels that open with a promise to answer a question or close an information gap, losing viewers between 10-20% of the video's runtime was associated with significantly worse distribution. The mechanism: YouTube's algorithm likely interprets early dropoff after the hook as a sign the video failed to deliver on its opening promise, and suppresses it accordingly. Losing people in the first 10% was surprisingly associated with more views, possibly because those viewers were never going to watch anyway and their quick exit didn't count against the video. The 10-20% window is where promise…
move: On promise-driven Shorts, measure where your dropoff happens frame-by-frame. If you're bleeding viewers between 10-20%, your payoff likely lands too late or disappoints. Test moving your biggest reveal or answer forward to the 5-10% mark instead of after the hook.

headline: X's new AI ranking model predicts time-spent instead of engagement actions
stat: ranker switched to time-spent prediction
statContext: the new retrieval and ranking model deployed in October 2026, no sample size disclosed
why: X's head of engineering said the new model predicts 'probable time spent' rather than discrete actions like likes or shares. The shift moves ranking away from countable engagement toward attention, meaning a clip that holds viewers without prompting a share could now rank higher than one that gets quick likes. The post did not define 'SI' in 'AI/SI model' or give precision numbers, so the degree of change is unclear. This contradicts the August weight file where shares had 40x the weight of dwell.
move: Test clips that maximize watch time without a call to action, and measure whether reach changes compared to your usual share-optimized hooks. If time-spent truly dominates now, a self-contained story that people watch through beats a cliffhanger that prompts a quick share.

headline: YouTube expanded A/B testing beyond thumbnails to entire video cuts and opening hooks
stat: native A/B testing now covers full video cuts
statContext: YouTube's new testing infrastructure announced in research summary dated October 2026
why: YouTube previously let creators test titles and thumbnails but not the video itself. The platform now runs native tests on different cuts and opening hooks, optimizing for watch time share and viewer retention rather than just clicks. This means YouTube is acknowledging that the first few seconds determine whether the algorithm spreads a Short, and it is giving creators the tooling to iterate on hooks at the platform level instead of guessing from aggregate analytics.
move: If you have YouTube Studio access, test two versions of your next Short with different opening lines or B-roll in the first three seconds, and let YouTube measure which one holds viewers longer. Use retention curves to find the exact drop-off point.

headline: Instagram third or later reposts of same clip hit 1,000 views zero times in 205-post sample
stat: 0% hit rate for 3rd+ posts versus 6% for first posts
statContext: 205 third-or-later Instagram reposts of the same source clip, posted Sept 28 to Oct 22, 2026, compared to 386 first posts
why: Instagram appears to fingerprint content and suppress clips it has already distributed, even if posted weeks apart by the same account. First posts of a clip zeroed 3% of the time, second posts 20%, and third or later posts hit 1,000 views zero times. The pattern did not hold on YouTube Shorts where third-to-fifth reposts still hit 1,000 views half the time. The mechanism is likely content-ID matching rather than a time penalty, since fresh debates from the same creator still performed. This confirms Instagram penalizes repeats more aggressively than other platforms.
move: Cap Instagram at two posts per source clip. If a debate or interview segment has already gone out twice on Instagram, hold it and post something from a different recording instead. Track which clips are repeats in your upload sheet so you see the empty slot rather than wondering why a post died.

headline: YouTube introduced dedicated Shorts Series infrastructure for organizing vertical videos into seasons
stat: new Shorts Series product launched
statContext: YouTube product announcement covered in October 2026 research summary
why: YouTube added native support for creators to organize Shorts into connected, bingeable series with season structure. This is YouTube validating the microdrama format where viewers watch multiple related Shorts in sequence, and it suggests the platform will start recommending the next Short in a series more aggressively than unrelated clips. The move signals YouTube is competing with TikTok's episodic content and wants to keep viewers in one creator's catalog rather than bouncing across the platform.
move: If you are cutting a long podcast into multiple Shorts, structure them as an explicit series in YouTube Studio instead of uploading them as unrelated clips. Test whether later episodes in a series get a reach boost from viewers finishing the first one.

headline: X algorithm dedupes video carousel by creator and semantic ID
stat: video carousel author dedupe on, semantic-ID dedupe level 0 to 3
statContext: default config changes in commit 862a123 pushed Oct 17, 2026 02:44 Berlin time
why: X wants one strong clip per creator instead of carousel flooding. The author dedupe stops multiple videos from the same account stacking in 'Videos for you'. The semantic-ID dedupe collapses near-duplicate and look-alike clips even from different accounts. Both changes punish reposting and reward original content. A test called ZeroFavCodivert also starts gating which brand-new, zero-like posts get initial reach, though it is off by default. The carousel also drops entirely if a 'Who to follow' module appears in the same response.
move: Post one strong original vertical clip instead of flooding the carousel with copies or slight variants. If you have been reposting the same clip multiple times, stop: the dedupe will collapse them and you will lose carousel slots.

headline: YouTube Shorts suppresses channels that mostly repost other creators' clips
stat: channels mostly re-uploading others' videos get less Shorts feed distribution
statContext: YouTube statement to creators Oct 2026, applies to vertical swipe feed reach
why: YouTube already blocked monetization from re-uploaded Shorts views before Oct 1. Now re-uploads also cost organic reach in the Shorts feed. The platform wants to push original content and stop creators from building channels on compilations or reuploads without significant transformation. YouTube did not publish a start date, a threshold for how much change counts as original, or a Studio metric showing whether your reach was cut. A channel that shifts to original content gets re-evaluated, but the timeline is unclear. The reach penalty applies at the channel level, like the monetization rule.
move: Audit your Shorts library this week. If most of your uploads are clips you collected or lightly edited from other creators, shift to original shoots or add substantial commentary and transformation. YouTube is vague about the line, so err toward more original work.

headline: X drops video quality view weight to zero, raises dwell weight to 0.05
stat: video quality view weight 0.05 to 0.0, dwell weight 0.0 to 0.05
statContext: ranking weight defaults in X's open-source code, commit Aug 25, 2026, still 0.0 on Oct 4
why: X's ranker predicts whether a viewer will give a video a quality view (watch past some threshold), then multiplies that probability by the VQV weight. Dropping the weight to zero means finishing a video no longer directly helps its For You score. At the same time, the dwell weight (stopping on the post without a specific action) went from zero to 0.05. X also restricts VQV credit to videos longer than 10 seconds, so a 9-second clip could never earn it even if the weight returned. The shift suggests X cares more about stopping the scroll than completing the watch. A clip climbs For You when…
move: Design your clips to stop the thumb in the first two seconds, not to hold to the end. A 15-second clip that gets shared beats a 90-second clip people finish but never send. Front-load the payoff and the share trigger. The platform is telling you retention is not the goal anymore.

headline: Instagram Reels under 3 minutes get same views; over 3 minutes lose 40%
stat: Reels over 3 minutes got 40% fewer views than shorter Reels
statContext: study of over 7,200 Reels by Sociable AI, date of sample not disclosed
why: Instagram's Reels ranker calculates a relevance score for about 100 candidates every time someone opens Reels, then shows them in order. Two signals are how many users watched at least 3 seconds and how many skipped within 2 seconds. The 3-minute threshold likely reflects where Instagram's system predicts lower completion or higher skip rates. Reels from 15 seconds to 3 minutes performed about the same on views. Longer Reels did earn more comments per view: 2-to-3-minute Reels got 65% more comments per view than 15-to-30-second Reels, suggesting they attract more invested viewers even if they…
move: If you want reach, keep Reels under 3 minutes. If you want deeper engagement and can accept lower view counts, try 2-to-3-minute pieces. Do not go over 3 minutes unless comments matter more than impressions for your goal this month.

headline: X's ranker raised not-interested penalty from 86 likes to 95 and cut bare-tap weight by a third
stat: not-interested went from -43.2 to -47.52, tap-in dropped from 0.4 to 0.3
statContext: weight changes in X's open-source ranking code committed September 29, 2026
why: X is distinguishing between passive taps and genuine engagement. A tap that holds attention for 10+ seconds now counts (0.4 weight, newly added), making the total tap-plus-dwell worth 0.7 of a like instead of the old bare-tap value of 0.8. Meanwhile the not-interested penalty grew about 10%, meaning one negative signal now cancels roughly 95 likes instead of 86. The platform is steering away from click-bait taps toward posts that actually hold readers, and it is making content suppression more aggressive when users explicitly reject something.
move: Write hooks that reward the second read, not just the tap. The first line must earn the next ten seconds. Test whether your post holds attention in replies or quote discussion, not just whether it got opened. One not-interested costs you nearly a hundred likes now, so avoid anything that looks like spam or rage-bait to even a small share of viewers.

headline: YouTube Shorts views now count from first frame, engagement views exclude loops for revenue
stat: views count from frame one as of August 24, 2026; engaged views exclude replays
statContext: view-counting rule change affecting all YouTube formats and Shorts revenue calculation
why: YouTube unified view counting across all formats on August 24, 2026: every play registers immediately with no minimum watch threshold. Shorts had already dropped the watch-time floor in March 2025, but this extended it platform-wide. The change separates vanity metrics from money: total views include loops and instant skips, but engaged views—the metric YouTube pays on and uses for Partner Program eligibility—count only viewers who stayed past the first seconds and exclude replays. YouTube defines engaged view as clicking to watch or watching past initial seconds. This means loop-optimized…
move: Stop designing Shorts around loops. They pad your view count but do not increase revenue or help you qualify for monetization. Focus on hooks that keep first-time viewers past the opening seconds, since that is what engaged views measure. Check your Average Percentage Viewed in Studio under Shorts analytics—it is calculated only from engaged views, so it shows whether your hook and pacing…

headline: TikTok videos of 3 to 10 minutes get 1.54x the views of 10-to-20 second clips from same creator
stat: 3-10 minute videos averaged 1.54x views, photo posts 0.81x, versus the same creator's 10-20 second videos
statContext: 3.2 million TikTok videos from 49,357 creators with 1,000+ followers, posted August 19 to September 2026
why: TikTok's algorithm appears to reward longer content that holds attention, contradicting the common advice to keep everything under 30 seconds. The dataset compared each creator's videos against their own other videos from the same month, isolating format effects from audience differences. Videos in the 3-10 minute range significantly outperformed short clips, while photo carousels underperformed at 0.81x. The likely mechanism: TikTok's ranking heavily weights watch time and completion rate, and a longer video that keeps even 40% of viewers delivers more absolute watch seconds than a 15-second…
move: Test videos in the 2-5 minute range if your content can sustain attention that long. Plan a narrative arc with multiple peaks instead of a single hook-payoff structure. Monitor your average watch time in TikTok Studio, not just completion rate—a 4-minute video watched halfway through delivers more ranking signal than a 20-second video watched fully. This does not mean pad everything; it means use…

headline: Instagram Reels ranker predicts resharing slightly more heavily for viewers who do not follow you
stat: resharing weighted slightly more important for unconnected content than for followers
statContext: Instagram head Adam Mosseri statement January 2025, confirmed in Meta system card 2026
why: Instagram uses two different weighting schemes depending on whether the viewer follows you. For followers, the ranking predictions are roughly balanced across watch time, likes, and sends. For non-followers—the audience that determines whether a Reel breaks out beyond your base—resharing (sends via DM) gets weighted slightly higher. Meta's 2026 system card phrases it as predicting whether you will reshare or share, and Mosseri explicitly said sends are slightly more important for unconnected content. The mechanism: Instagram wants to surface Reels that people actively pass along to friends…
move: Write Reels that give viewers a reason to send them to a specific person. Test whether your hook or concept creates a this-is-you moment or solves a problem someone would DM to a friend. Check your sends-per-reach in Instagram Insights under Interactions—it is the signal Instagram weights most for expanding beyond your follower base. A Reel that gets shared travels faster than one that just gets…

headline: YouTube Shorts dropped minimum watch requirement for view counting in March 2025
stat: views count from first play, no minimum watch time
statContext: all Shorts views since March 2025, down from previous threshold
why: YouTube removed the watch-time floor that separated a counted view from a skip. This aligns Shorts counting with TikTok and Instagram, where a view fires immediately. The change makes vanity metrics rise but does not affect ranking—YouTube still weights satisfaction surveys and retention for recommendations. The timing matters because it preceded the August 24 threshold drop across all formats and the October 1 originality update, suggesting YouTube was systematically simplifying its counting rules before tightening quality filters.
move: Stop using raw view counts as a success signal for Shorts. Track click-through from impressions and average watch percentage instead, since those still predict whether YouTube promotes the video.

headline: YouTube began ranking original Shorts higher and suppressing re-uploads on October 1
stat: original content prioritised, re-uploads without added value get less reach
statContext: YouTube Shorts feed recommendations starting October 1, 2026
why: YouTube updated its recommendation systems to 'further prioritize original content and reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own'. The mechanism is a new originality classifier in the ranker, not just duplicate detection—YouTube is judging whether you added creative value. This follows the March view-counting change and suggests YouTube is fighting the TikTok repost farms that flooded Shorts after monetisation opened. The move was predictable (every platform eventually does this) but the timing—right before the February 2027 revenue…
move: If you remix or compile others' clips, add substantive commentary, new editing or a unique angle. If you cannot add value, do not post it. Check your Shorts feed impressions in Analytics after October 1—a drop with stable CTR and retention means you were flagged.

headline: X's video-open weight rose from 0.05 to 0.07 while video quality view dropped to zero
stat: video_open weight 0.05 to 0.07, vqv weight 0.05 to 0.0
statContext: X's Phoenix ranking model default weights, commit on August 25, 2026
why: X simultaneously raised the credit for opening a video player and eliminated the bonus for watching to a quality threshold. The mechanism: X is rewarding the click more than the finish, which inverts typical short-form logic. This pairs with the binary dwell change (also August 25)—X now pays for initial interest (the open) and sustained attention (10-second dwell), but not for passive completion. The likely reason: completion is too easy to game with ultra-short clips, while open+dwell together signal real intent. The move contradicts creator advice to 'just make them watch to the end'.
move: For video on X: optimise your thumbnail and first frame to drive the open, then script the first ten seconds to hold attention through the dwell threshold. Stop worrying about finishing the clip—there is no ranking credit for it anymore.

headline: X accounts posting over 10 times daily see roughly 14% lower engagement per post
stat: 14% lower engagement per post above 10 posts/day
statContext: brand accounts in one third-party posting-frequency analysis, date not specified
why: This is audience fatigue, not an algorithmic penalty. The same follower base cannot engage with every post when volume is high, so each additional post past the ceiling returns less. The mechanism: your followers' feeds fill with your content, they skip more of it, and the ranker sees lower predicted engagement on each piece. The finding contradicts 'post as much as possible' advice but aligns with X's reply/retweet-heavy ranking—conversations need time to develop. The source is thin (one unnamed analysis, no date, no methodology), so treat this as a rough benchmark, not a law.
move: If you post more than 10 times a day, audit whether each post is genuinely earning replies and shares. If engagement per post is dropping, cut frequency and raise quality—fewer posts that spark conversation will outrank more posts that get passive likes.

headline: X's ranker now rewards ten-second click-dwell instead of passive impressions
stat: click-dwell weight set to 1.0 in default config, binary trigger at 10 seconds
statContext: X's Phoenix ranker configuration as of September 2026, affects how clicks on posts are scored
why: X added a click-dwell head that only fires positive if the viewer stays at least ten seconds after clicking. This replaces the old model where any click counted equally. The mechanism: a viewer who clicks a link and bounces after four seconds fires nothing; one who stays eleven seconds fires the head. This aligns with the August 25 binary dwell change—X is systematically rewarding attention duration over passive actions. The platform wants engagement that holds people on-platform or demonstrates genuine interest, not reflexive taps.
move: If you share links, write captions that make people want to stay and discuss rather than immediately clicking through. Test posting the link in a reply instead of the main post so the click-through doesn't kill the parent post's distribution.

headline: X's Phoenix aggregation switched from short dwell to long dwell as the default
stat: aggregation default changed from short dwell to long dwell
statContext: X's Phoenix ranking system configuration change, affects how dwell time signals are processed
why: The Phoenix aggregation setting controls how dwell signals are rolled up across a user's session. Switching the default from short to long dwell means the ranker now prioritizes sustained attention over quick glances. This is the third dwell-related change in the same update (binary dwell turned on, dwell weight raised to 0.05, and now this aggregation switch). The pattern is clear: X is systematically retuning every part of the ranking system that touches attention duration. Long dwell likely means they're measuring across a longer time window or weighting later seconds more heavily than the…
move: Optimize the first thirty seconds to hold attention, not just the first three. If you make threads, make the second and third posts worth reading—X may now be crediting you for keeping someone in the thread longer.

headline: X weights scale predicted probabilities not raw counts, one report does not cancel hundreds of likes
stat: weights multiply the viewer's own predicted probability of each action
statContext: Explanation of how X's ranking weights work in the open-source code, clarifies common misconception
why: The ranking weights people see in X's code—like report at -1.5 and like at 0.5—do not mean one report literally cancels three likes. They scale the predicted probability that this specific viewer will take that action, which is calculated from the viewer's own past behavior. A viewer who never reports anything has a near-zero report probability, so even a high negative weight barely moves their score. This matters because it means controversial posts that get both loves and hates are not simply averaged—the system predicts whether you personally will like or report it based on your history…
move: Stop worrying about getting reported by people who were never going to engage positively. Focus on creating content that your actual audience—the people whose behavior predicts they will engage—wants to see. Polarization is not inherently penalized if the right half loves it.

headline: TikTok judges each video independently; same account's best and worst posts differ massively in reach
stat: 58 creators' best vs worst recent posts showed wide variance within same account
statContext: September 2026 sample via TokConnect of ten recent posts each across six niches
why: If TikTok's algorithm penalized or boosted at the account level, one creator's videos would cluster around a similar view count. They do not. The same account can have one video hit 500K and the next hit 8K. This confirms what TikTok has said but creators often doubt: the algorithm does not remember your last video's performance when ranking the new one. Each video enters the same cold-start test regardless of whether your previous post flopped or went viral. The mechanism is economic—TikTok wants to fill the For You feed with the best content right now, and past performance is a weak…
move: Do not let a low-performing video discourage you from posting the next one. Each video gets a fair shot. Test more concepts rather than trying to reverse-engineer why the last one failed—the algorithm does not care about your last one.

headline: X raised video-open weight and turned on binary dwell while killing quality-view finish bonus
stat: video_open weight went 0.05 to 0.07, dwell went 0.0 to 0.05, vqv went 0.05 to 0.0
statContext: Three of twenty-six ranking weights in X's open-source algorithm, changed August 25, 2026
why: X stopped rewarding finish rates and started rewarding the open itself plus binary dwell (whether you stayed at all, not how long). The video_open head is the only weight X has raised from a nonzero value in the published history since August 13. The mechanism appears to be a shift from completion-based signals to attention-holding signals: you now get paid for the open and for keeping someone on the post, but not for them reaching a quality-view threshold. This contradicts the common advice to optimize for finish rate on X video.
move: For X video, optimize the first three seconds to prevent an immediate swipe-away rather than building to a payoff that rewards completion. The dwell head now pays what the finish bonus used to pay.

headline: Off-platform links in X posts showed 33% fewer median likes in 21,864-post sample
stat: 33% fewer median likes
statContext: 2,626 posts with genuine off-platform links versus posts without them, from 7,829 accounts over 236 days, relevance-ranked sample
why: The headline number appears in a researcher-audited observational study that corrected for a methodological error: searching post text for 'http' showed a positive association, but filtering for genuine off-platform destination hosts showed negative. The study itself does not claim this proves an algorithmic penalty—linked posts may differ in intent, topic, format, author, and audience. X's For You feed uses many personalized signals, not a single public link multiplier. The mechanism is likely selection bias: people write different kinds of posts when they include links, and those posts attra
move: Test links in your own account rather than treating this as a universal rule. The same study found linked posts got fewer views but more bookmarks, which suggests they serve a reference function rather than a reach function.

headline: Replies and retweets outweigh likes roughly 2-to-1 in X's open-source ranking weights
stat: retweet weighted 1.0, like weighted 0.5
statContext: Weights from X's 2023 open-sourced ranking code, widely cited across third-party analyses
why: X open-sourced its For You ranking code in 2023 and the relative weights have been public since then, so this is not new. The mechanism is that X's algorithm treats engagement types as predictions of future engagement: a retweet exposes the post to a new network, so it signals broader appeal. A like is private feedback. The code also shows negative actions (blocks, reports, mutes) carry weights several times larger than positive ones in the opposite direction, which means suppression is faster than amplification.
move: Optimize posts for replies and retweets, not just likes. Ask a question, make a claim people want to argue with, or write something people want to add to. A single retweet is worth roughly two likes in the ranking system.

headline: LinkedIn posts with 61+ seconds dwell hit 15.6% engagement versus 1.2% for 0-3 seconds
stat: 15.6% engagement rate at 61+ seconds dwell versus 1.2% at 0-3 seconds
statContext: AuthoredUp dataset, sample size not disclosed, LinkedIn officially documents dwell time as a top signal
why: LinkedIn officially names dwell time as the one feed signal it documents in depth, and this third-party dataset quantifies the relationship. The mechanism is that LinkedIn's three-stage ranking flow (spam filter, small-sample engagement test, network-relevance ranking) uses dwell as a proxy for content quality: if someone stops scrolling to read, the system infers the post is worth showing to more people in that person's network. Thoughtful comments amplify this further. The pattern was already widely known among LinkedIn creators.
move: Write posts that earn long dwell time: open with a hook that makes someone stop scrolling, then deliver enough substance that they stay for a minute. Use line breaks and short paragraphs so the post looks readable at a glance.
